summary:
Project Neotegrals is a tool that will make it much easier for astronomers to search for Planet X or moving celestial bodies due to the fact that the project will unify separate astronomical datasets in one simple interface and thus accelerate the research process. The problem today is that decades' worth of infrared and optical sky surveys can be found only in separate and complicated databases.
To solve the issue and simplify multi-epoch observation, our platform offers real multi-decade imagery (DSS2, 2MASS, WISE, Pan-STARRS) along with NASA’s SPHEREx data. With help of our Compare and Blink Epochs tools users can observe precisely the same coordinates in different years and see how the stars move against the background – moving objects, brown dwarfs and possible candidates to become Planet X become clearly visible to the naked eye. Users can mark moving dots to get their coordinates, use parallax shift calculator and monitor benchmark challenges like WISE 0855 and Barnard's star.
Moreover, the platform has the Hubble catalog of 13,000 deep space objects, guide to the 102 spectral bands of SPHEREx and orbit visualization of interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS using 259 real IRSA spectral images (which matched predicted positions with median of 0.02°).
details:
Team Neotegrals have developed an interactive astronomical exploration and citizen science platform to address a very real problem in the field of space science: the sheer scale of sky surveys and mission data over the decades, which is all stored in a number of disparate and very difficult to navigate archives. Their web app brings together real historical and current observations (DSS2, 2MASS, WISE, Pan-STARRS, Hubble, SPHEREx etc) into a single, easy to use sky map which can be searched by object name or by coordinates.

Key features include:

Multi-epoch Blink & Compare modes: you can view four frames of exactly the same patch of sky, taken at different times (decades apart). The distant background stars will of course be fixed in position, but any nearby fast-moving objects (brown dwarfs, high proper motion stars and potential Planet X's) will be seen to jump. You can simply click on any of the moving objects to record and save their coordinates for citizen science.

SPHEREx 102-Colour Explorer: an interactive guide to the SPHEREx mission, its 102 infrared spectral bands (0.75 to 5 microns) and what each band tells us, with actual NASA all-sky images.

Planet X Parallax Calculator and Benchmark Targets: an interactive calculator which shows the parallax of an object (how far it moves across the sky over a 6 month baseline) as a function of its distance (the fundamental geometry of the Planet X detection scenario). You can also look at the motion tracks for 5 benchmark targets: WISE 0855, Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, RW Aurigae and R Draconis.

Interstellar Comet 3I/ATLAS live orbit: Using the actual SPHEREx observation tables from IRSA (259 spectral images over 133 exposures from Aug 1–15 and Dec 8-14 2025), our platform plots each exposure onto the sky map. Our independently derived orbit agrees with the positions predicted by the SPHEREx science team to a median accuracy of 0.02 degrees.

Deep Sky Catalog, Planetary Timelapses and Methodology: A searchable catalog of around 13,000 deep sky objects complete with NASA Hubble descriptions, planetary motion timelapses and a Method tab which details all data sources, all the scientific formulae and all the credits.

Benefits & Intended Impact

By removing the very steep technical hurdle of having to query raw FITS files and the various agency portals, our platform effectively opens up real space data to everyone. It enables students, teachers and amateur astronomers to actually see parallax, proper motion and infrared spectroscopy for themselves and turns learning from a passive activity into an active form of citizen science.

Tools, Languages & Software Used

Frontend: HTML, CSS, TypeScript (for the interactive sky map rendering, multi-frame sync and UI controls).

Backend: JavaScript (Node.js) for the astronomical catalog queries, the coordinate transformations and the orbital/parallax calculations.

Data and scientific sources: NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), SPHEREx mission data, Hubble Space Telescope catalogues, DSS2, 2MASS, WISE and Pan-STARRS.

Creativity & Factors Considered

Creative approach: rather than just hand out some static tables or some complex command line tool, we've blended the classic astronomical "blink comparator" technique with modern 4-panel web visualisation and live orbital verification of 3I/ATLAS.

Key factors considered: scientific accuracy (we've checked our orbital maths against the official SPHEREx predictions), visual clarity (we've got all the multi-survey epochs lined up properly), ease of use for the novice via the inbuilt explanations and, of course, full attribution of all the public NASA data sets we've used.

Data Attribution: This publication makes use of data products from the Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer (SPHEREx), a joint project of JPL and the California Institute of Technology and funded by NASA.
